differences.title: No main, no setup
differences.text: Statements at the top level run immediately, in order. The compiler is part of the operating system, so the prompt, scripts and programs all use one language.

differences.title: A string statement prints
differences.text: A bare string literal is a statement that prints it; extra values after commas fill the % codes. Print(...) does the same explicitly.

differences.title: Sized type names
differences.text: U0, I8 to I64, U8 to U64 and F64 replace void, char, int, long and double.

differences.title: Calls without parentheses
differences.text: A function that needs no arguments can be called by its name alone.

differences.title: Default and skipped arguments
differences.text: A parameter can have a default, and a call can leave an argument out by keeping its comma.

differences.title: Inline assembly and the compiler as a service
differences.text: asm blocks sit inside HolyC code, and code can be compiled and run at run time because the compiler is always present.

differences.title: Classes with inheritance
differences.text: class groups fields like a struct and can extend another class.

differences.title: A richer switch
differences.text: switch can contain start and end sections for sub-cases.

differences.title: Exceptions
differences.text: try, catch and throw exist; a thrown value is a short constant.

differences.title: $ is special in strings
differences.text: In text shown by the system, a dollar sign begins a document-format command, so a literal dollar is written twice.

differences.title: Operator precedence
differences.text: Some operators, notably the bitwise ones against the comparisons, bind in a different order from C. This site's interpreter uses C precedence, so avoid mixing them.
